stories.headline: OCTOBER PPI RISES 0.3%, ANNUAL RATE HITS 6.5% — HOTTEST SINCE 2022 — KEEPING FED ON TRACK TO HIKE
stories.body: The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported October producer prices rose 0.3% month-over-month, just under the 0.4% forecast, but the year-over-year rate jumped to 6.5%, the fastest pace since 2022; core PPI (ex-food and energy) rose 0.3% on the month and 5.0% annually, matching a rate last seen in January 2023, while the goods index surged 10.2% year-over-year, the biggest 12-month gain since October 2022.
stories.explain: PPI measures prices at the factory gate before they reach consumers, so a hot goods reading signals that cost pressure is still building upstream and likely to show up in CPI and core PCE in coming months rather than fading on its own. Combined with this week's hotter-than-expected core CPI, today's print gives the Fed's hawks fresh ammunition heading into the Dec. 8-9 meeting, which is why futures barely budged off the 82-85% odds of a quarter-point hike even as equities sold off.

stories.headline: NVIDIA CLOSES BELOW $4 TRILLION MARKET CAP FOR FIRST TIME SINCE JULY 2025 AS SIXTH STRAIGHT WEEKLY DECLINE DEEPENS
stories.body: Nvidia shares fell roughly 2% Friday, pushing the company's market capitalization below $4 trillion for the first time since July 2025 and extending its losing streak to six consecutive weeks — its longest since 2012 — as the fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation and HSBC's downgrade to Hold continued to weigh on the stock. Goldman Sachs called the leadership change a "meaningful, but measured negative" for the shares.
stories.explain: A stock shedding roughly 13% over a week while the underlying AI capex story hasn't changed tells you the market is repricing execution and governance risk, not demand — but because Nvidia alone carries a mid-to-high single-digit weight in both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100, that repricing mechanically subtracts from both indices regardless of what every other constituent does. That's the arithmetic behind why a single-company governance story is still the dominant driver of today's broad tape.

stories.headline: S&P 500 SLIPS 0.40% AS NASDAQ-100 DROPS 1.21% ON TECH ROTATION, BUT DOW ADVANCES ON THE DAY
stories.body: The S&P 500 fell 0.40% to 7,562 and the Nasdaq 100 dropped 1.21% to 27,944 as money rotated out of mega-cap tech and into cyclicals, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average posted a modest gain on the session. Despite Friday's pullback, the S&P 500 still finished the week higher after a string of gains earlier in the week.
stories.explain: A session where the Dow rises while the Nasdaq 100 falls more than a percent is a rotation signature, not a broad risk-off move — capital left concentrated, rate-sensitive tech names (hit by both the Nvidia story and firmer yields) and moved into value-oriented, less duration-sensitive sectors. That divergence between cap-weighted tech benchmarks and the broader market is exactly what you'd expect when a single large-cap governance shock collides with a hawkish inflation print on the same day.

stories.headline: DECEMBER HIKE ODDS HOLD NEAR 82-85% UNDER WARSH AS HOT PPI REINFORCES HAWKISH CASE
stories.body: Fed funds futures continued to price roughly an 82-85% probability of a quarter-point hike at the Dec. 8-9 FOMC meeting under Chair Kevin Warsh, with today's hotter-than-expected PPI print reinforcing rather than challenging that pricing after this week's hot core CPI reading.
stories.explain: When two consecutive inflation reports — CPI and now PPI — both surprise to the upside, the Fed's reaction function has less room to treat either as noise, because persistent upstream (producer) and downstream (consumer) price pressure together look like broadening inflation rather than a one-off. That's why hike odds held steady rather than spiking further: the market had already priced most of this outcome in, and the print simply removed the chance the Fed uses a soft PPI as an excuse to hold.

stories.headline: GOLD SLIPS 0.75% TO $3,888 AS DOLLAR AND YIELDS FIRM; WTI ADDS 0.76% TO $89 ON SUPPLY-SIDE SUPPORT
stories.body: Gold fell 0.75% to $3,888 an ounce as the dollar index (DXY) firmed 0.25% to 103.41 and the 10-year yield held near 5.15%, raising the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset; WTI crude bucked the broader move, adding 0.76% to $89 a barrel on supply-side factors distinct from today's rates and equity story.
stories.explain: Gold's decline is the mirror image of a firmer dollar and higher real yields: a stronger DXY makes gold costlier for non-dollar buyers, while elevated yields raise the carrying cost of a zero-coupon asset, so both moved against gold simultaneously today. Oil's gain despite that same hawkish backdrop indicates crude traders are responding to a supply-specific catalyst rather than the macro and equity-market narrative driving everything else.

watchlist: Nvidia's Q3 FY2027 earnings call, Nov. 17 — first major test of investor confidence under interim CEO Colette Kress after a sixth straight weekly decline and HSBC's downgrade to Hold
Fed's Dec. 8-9 FOMC meeting — hike odds near 82-85% under Chair Kevin Warsh after today's hot October PPI reinforced this week's hot core CPI
10-year Treasury yield near 5.15% — a further push higher would tighten financial conditions heading into the December decision
Nvidia's search for a permanent CEO after Jensen Huang's resignation — Huang reportedly willing to testify before Congress on the espionage allegations as soon as next week
November retail sales and jobs data — the next readings the Fed will weigh before the December meeting

deepDive.title: From Factory Gate to Fed Decision: What the PPI Actually Tells You About Where CPI Is Headed
content: Today's biggest data release wasn't a surprise in direction, only in magnitude: October's Producer Price Index rose 6.5% year-over-year, the fastest pace since 2022, landing two days after a hotter-than-expected core CPI print and the same week Nvidia's leadership shake-up has dominated the tape. Markets treated the PPI print as confirmation rather than new information, which is itself telling. Understanding why economists and traders watch PPI as a leading signal for CPI — rather than just another inflation number to shrug off — explains why today's print mattered more to Fed pricing than its modest headline miss (0.3% versus 0.4% expected) would suggest.

PPI measures prices received by producers for their output at the wholesale or factory-gate stage, before retailers add their own markups and pass costs to consumers; CPI measures what households actually pay at the register. Because production happens in stages — raw materials, intermediate goods, finished goods — rising costs tend to show up in PPI's earlier stages before they fully propagate to the finished-goods level consumers see, which is why PPI is often described as a leading indicator for CPI with a lag of one to several months. Today's core PPI, which excludes volatile food and energy, rose 5.0% annually, matching a rate last seen in January 2023 — a level the Fed's preferred core PCE gauge has not yet caught up to.

What's easy to miss is that not all of PPI feeds through evenly: the report's goods component jumped 10.2% year-over-year, the sharpest 12-month gain since October 2022, while services and trade margins moved far less. That goods-services gap matters because it points to where the pressure is concentrated — import-exposed and tariff-sensitive categories — rather than broad-based demand overheating. The 2021-2022 cycle is the closest precedent: PPI accelerated several months before CPI peaked, as supply-chain bottlenecks and input costs worked their way through inventories before hitting shelf prices, a pattern the Fed initially underestimated and then had to catch up to with faster tightening.

That history is exactly why today's print reinforced rather than reset December hike odds near 82-85%: a Fed that remembers being behind the curve in 2021-2022 is unlikely to treat two consecutive hot inflation reports — CPI then PPI — as noise, especially with the goods component suggesting the pressure has further to travel downstream. For a student watching this unfold, the lesson is to track PPI's goods and core components specifically, not just the year-over-year headline, because that's the piece most likely to show up in November and December CPI readings and ultimately in the data the Fed's Summary of Economic Projections will reflect at its Dec. 8-9 meeting.
